Reconfiguration of Non-crossing Spanning Trees

Oswin Aichholzer Affiliation: University of Technology Graz, Austria. oaich@ist.tugraz.at    Brad Ballinger Affiliation: Cal Poly Humboldt, USA. brad@humboldt.edu    Therese Biedl Affiliation: University of Waterloo, Canada. {biedl,alubiw,jayson.lynch}@uwaterloo.ca    Mirela Damian Affiliation: Villanova University, USA. mirela.damian@villanova.edu    Erik D. Demaine Affiliation: MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, USA. edemaine@mit.edu    Matias Korman Affiliation: Siemens Electronic Design Automation, USA. matias_korman@mentor.com    Anna Lubiw Affiliation: University of Waterloo, Canada. {biedl,alubiw,jayson.lynch}@uwaterloo.ca    Jayson Lynch Affiliation: University of Waterloo, Canada. {biedl,alubiw,jayson.lynch}@uwaterloo.ca    Josef Tkadlec Affiliation: Harvard Unversity, USA. tkadlec@math.harvard.edu    Yushi Uno Affiliation: Osaka Metropolitan University, Japan. yushi.uno@omu.ac.jp
Abstract

For a set PP of nn points in the plane in general position, a non-crossing spanning tree is a spanning tree of the points where every edge is a straight-line segment between a pair of points and no two edges intersect except at a common endpoint. We study the problem of reconfiguring one non-crossing spanning tree of PP to another using a sequence of flips where each flip removes one edge and adds one new edge so that the result is again a non-crossing spanning tree of PP. There is a known upper bound of 2​n−42n-4 flips [Avis and Fukuda, 1996] and a lower bound of 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips.

We give a reconfiguration algorithm that uses at most 2​n−32n-3 flips but reduces that to 1.5​n−21.5n-2 flips when one tree is a path and either: the points are in convex position; or the path is monotone in some direction. For points in convex position, we prove an upper bound of 2​d−Ω⁡(log⁡d)2d-\Omega(\log d) where dd is half the size of the symmetric difference between the trees. We also examine whether the happy edges (those common to the initial and final trees) need to flip, and we find exact minimum flip distances for small point sets using exhaustive search.

1 Introduction

Let PP be a set of nn points in the plane in general position. A non-crossing spanning tree is a spanning tree of PP whose edges are straight line segments between pairs of points such that no two edges intersect except at a common endpoint. A reconfiguration step or flip removes one edge of a non-crossing spanning tree and adds one new edge so that the result is again a non-crossing spanning tree of PP. We study the problem of reconfiguring one non-crossing spanning of PP to another via a sequence of flips.

Researchers often consider three problems about reconfiguration, which are most easily expressed in terms of the reconfiguration graph that has a vertex for each configuration (in our case, each non-crossing spanning tree) and an edge for each reconfiguration step. The problems are: (1) connectivity of the reconfiguration graph—is reconfiguration always possible? (2) diameter of the reconfiguration graph—how many flips are needed for reconfiguration in the worst case? and (3) distance in the reconfiguration graph—what is the complexity of finding the minimum number of flips to reconfigure between two given configurations?

For reconfiguration of non-crossing spanning trees, Avis and Fukuda [10, Section 3.7] proved that reconfiguration is always possible, and that at most 2​n−42n-4 flips are needed. Hernando et al. [20] proved a lower bound of 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips. Even for the special case of points in convex position, there are no better upper or lower bounds known.

Our two main results make some progress in reducing the diameter upper bounds.

(1) For points in general position, we give a reconfiguration algorithm that uses at most 2​n−32n-3 flips but reduces that to 1.5​n−21.5n-2 flips in two cases: (1) when the points are in convex position and one tree is a path; (2) for general point sets when one tree is a monotone path. The algorithm first flips one tree to a downward tree (with each vertex connected to a unique higher vertex) and the other tree to an upward tree (defined symmetrically) using n−2n-2 flips—this is where we save when one tree is a path. After that, we give an algorithm to flip from a downward tree TDT_{D} to an upward tree TUT_{U} using at most n−1n-1 “perfect” flips each of which removes an edge of TDT_{D} and adds an edge of TUT_{U}. The algorithm is simple to describe, but proving that intermediate trees remain non-crossing is non-trivial. We also show that 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips may be required, even in the two special cases. See Section 2.

(2) For points in convex position, we improve the upper bound on the number of required flips to 2​d−Ω⁡(log⁡d)2d-\Omega(\log d) where dd is half the size of the symmetric difference between the trees. So dd flips are needed in any flip sequence, and 2​d2d is an upper bound. The idea is to find an edge ee of one tree that is crossed by at most (roughly) d/2d/2 edges of the other tree, flip all but one of the crossing edges temporarily to the convex hull (this will end up costing 2 flips per edge), and then flip the last crossing edge to ee. Repeating this saves us one flip, compared to the 2​d2d bound, for each of the (roughly) log⁡d\log d repetitions. See Section 3.

Notably, neither of our algorithms uses the common—but perhaps limited—technique of observing that the diameter is at most twice the radius, and bounding the radius of the reconfiguration graph by identifying a “canonical” configuration that every other configuration can be flipped to. Rather, our algorithms find reconfiguration sequences tailored to the specific input trees.

In hopes of making further progress on the diameter and distance problems, we address the question of which edges need to be involved in a minimum flip sequence from an initial non-crossing spanning tree TIT_{I} to a final non-crossing spanning tree TFT_{F}. We say that the edges of TI∩TFT_{I}\cap T_{F} are happy edges, and we formulate the Happy Edge Conjecture that for points in convex position, there is a minimum flip sequence that never flips happy edges. We prove the conjecture for happy convex hull edges. See Section 4. More generally, we say that a reconfiguration problem has the “happy element property” if elements that are common to the initial and final configurations can remain fixed in a minimum flip sequence. Reconfiguration problems that satisfy the happy element property seem easier. For example, the happy element property holds for reconfiguring spanning trees in a graph (and indeed for matroids more generally), and the distance problem is easy. On the other hand, the happy element property fails for reconfiguring triangulations of a point set in the plane, and for the problem of token swapping on a tree [12], and in both cases, this is the key to constructing gadgets to prove that the distance problem is NP-hard [26, 31, 4]. As an aside, we note that for reconfiguring triangulations of a set of points in convex position—where the distance problem is the famous open question of rotation distance in binary trees—the happy element property holds [35], which may be why no one has managed to prove that the distance problem is NP-hard.

Finally, we implemented a combinatorial search program to compute the diameter (maximum reconfiguration distance between two trees) and radius of the reconfiguration graph for points in convex position. For 6≤n≤126\leq n\leq 12 the diameter is ⌊1.5​n−4⌋\lfloor 1.5n-4\rfloor and the radius is n−2n-2. In addition we provide the same information for the special case when the initial and final trees are non-crossing spanning paths, though intermediate configurations may be more general trees. We also verify the Happy Edge Conjecture for n≤10n\leq 10 points in convex position. See Section 5.

1.1 Background and Related Results

Reconfiguration is about changing one structure to another, either through continuous motion or through discrete changes. In mathematics, the topic has a vast and deep history, for example in knot theory, and the study of bounds on the simplex method for linear programming. Recently, reconfiguration via discrete steps has become a focused research area, see the surveys by van den Heuvel [36] and Nishimura [29]. Examples include sorting a list by swapping pairs of adjacent elements, solving a Rubik’s cube, or changing one colouring of a graph to another. With discrete reconfiguration steps, the reconfiguration graph is well-defined. Besides questions of diameter and distance in the reconfiguration graph, there is also research on enumeration via a Hamiltonian cycle in the reconfiguration graph, see the recent survey [27], and on mixing properties to find random configurations, see [33].

Our work is about reconfiguring one graph to another. Various reconfiguration steps have been considered, for example exchanging one vertex for another (for reconfiguration of paths [14], independent sets [23, 11], etc.), or exchanging multiple edges (for reconfiguration of matchings [13]). However, we concentrate on elementary steps (often called edge flips) that exchange one edge for one other edge. A main example of this is reconfiguring one spanning tree of a graph to another, which can always be accomplished by “perfect” flips that add an edge of the final tree and delete an edge of the initial tree—more generally, such a perfect exchange sequence is possible when reconfiguring bases of a matroid.

Our focus is on geometric graphs whose vertices are points in the plane and whose edges are non-crossing line segments between the points. In this setting, one well-studied problem is reconfiguring between triangulations of a point set in the plane, see the survey by Bose and Hurtado [15]. Here, a flip replaces an edge in a convex quadrilateral by the other diagonal of the quadrilateral. For the special case of nn points in convex position this is equivalent to rotation of an edge in a given (abstract) rooted binary tree, which is of interest in the study of splay trees, and the study of phylogenetic trees in computational biology. While an upper bound for the reconfiguration distance of 2​n−102n-10 is known to be tight for n>12n>12 [32, 35], the complexity of computing the shortest distance between two triangulations of a convex point set (equivalently between two given binary trees) is still unknown. See [6, 26, 31] for related hardness results for the flip-distance of triangulations of point sets and simple polygons.

Another well-studied problem for geometric graphs is reconfiguration of non-crossing perfect matchings. Here a flip typically exchanges matching and non-matching edges in non-crossing cycles, and there are results for a single cycle of unbounded length [21], and for multiple cycles [3, 34]. For points in convex position, the flip operation on a single cycle of length 4 suffices to connect the reconfiguration graph [19], but this is open for general point sets. For a more general flip operation that connects any two disjoint matchings whose union is non-crossing, the reconfiguration graph is connected for points in convex position [1] (and, notably, the diameter is less than twice the radius), but connectivity is open for general point sets [3, 22].

The specific geometric graphs we study are non-crossing (or “plane”) spanning trees of a set of points in the plane. For points in convex position, these have been explored for enumeration [30], and for a duality with quadrangulations and consequent lattice properties, e.g., see [9] and related literature.

For non-crossing spanning trees of a general point set in the plane, there are several basic reconfiguration operations that can be used to transform these trees into each other. The one we use in this work is the simple edge exchange of an edge ee by an edge e′e^{\prime} as described above. If we require that ee and e′e^{\prime} do not cross, then this operation is called a compatible edge exchange. Even more restricted is an edge rotation, where e=u​ve=uv and e′=u​we^{\prime}=uw share a common vertex uu. If the triangle u,v,wu,v,w is not intersected by an edge of the two involved trees, then this is called an empty triangle edge rotation. The most restricted operation is the edge slide (see also Section 4.3) where the edge v​wvw has to exist in both trees. The name comes from viewing this transformation as sliding one end of the edge ee along v​wvw to e′e^{\prime} (and rotating the other end around uu) and at no time crossing through any other edge of the trees. For an overview and detailed comparison of the described operations see Nichols et al. [28].

It has been shown that the reconfiguration graph of non-crossing spanning trees is even connected for the “as-local-as-possible” edge slide operation [2]. See also [7] where a tight bound of Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) steps for the diameter is show. This implies that also for the other reconfiguration operations the flip graph is connected. For edge exchange, compatible edge exchange, and edge rotation a linear upper bound for the diameter is known [10], while for empty triangle edge rotations an upper bound of O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) has been shown recently [28]. For all operations (except edge slides) the best known lower bound is 1.5​n−51.5n-5 [20].

There are several variants for the reconfiguration of spanning trees. For example, the operations can be performed in parallel, that is, as long as the exchanges (slides etc) do not interfere with each other, they can be done in one step; see [28] for an overview of results. In a similar direction of a more global operation we can say that two non-crossing spanning trees are compatible, if their union is still crossing free. A single reconfiguration step then transforms one such tree into the other. A lower bound of Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega(\log n/\log\log n) [16] and an upper bound of O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) [2] for the diameter of this reconfiguration graph has been shown.

Another variation is that the edges are labeled (independent of the vertex labels), and if an edge is exchanged the replacement edge takes that label. In this way two geometrically identical trees can have a rather large transformation distance. For labeled triangulations there is a good characterization of when reconfiguration is possible, and a polynomial bound on the number of steps required [25].

The reconfiguration of non-crossing spanning paths (where each intermediate configuration must be a path) has also been considered. For points in convex position, the diameter of the reconfiguration graph is 2​n−62n-6 for n≥5n\geq 5 [8, 17]. Surprisingly, up to now it remains an open problem if the reconfiguration graph of non-crossing spanning paths is connected for general point sets [5].

1.2 Definitions and Terminology

Let PP be a set of nn points in general position, meaning that no three points are collinear. The points of PP are in convex position if the boundary of the convex hull of PP contains all the points of PP. An edge is a line segment joining two points of PP, and a spanning tree TT of PP is a set of n−1n-1 edges that form a tree. Two edges cross if they intersect but do not share a common endpoint. A non-crossing spanning tree is a spanning tree such that no two of its edges cross. When we write “two non-crossing spanning trees,” we mean that each tree is non-crossing but we allow edges of one tree to cross edges of the other tree.

We sometimes consider the special case where a non-crossing spanning tree of PP is a path. A path is monotone if there is a direction in the plane such that the order of points along the path matches the order of points in that direction.

For a spanning tree of a graph, a flip removes one edge and adds one new edge to obtain a new spanning tree, i.e., spanning trees TT and T′T^{\prime} are related by a flip if T′=T∖{e}∪{e′}T^{\prime}=T\setminus\{e\}\cup\{e^{\prime}\}, where e∈Te\in T and e′∉Te^{\prime}\notin T. The same definition applies to non-crossing spanning trees: If TT is a non-crossing spanning tree of PP, and T′=T∖{e}∪{e′}T^{\prime}=T\setminus\{e\}\cup\{e^{\prime}\} is a non-crossing spanning tree of PP, then we say that TT and T′T^{\prime} are related by a flip. We allow ee and e′e^{\prime} to cross.

Let TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} be initial and final non-crossing spanning trees of PP. A flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} is a sequence of flips that starts with TIT_{I} and ends with TFT_{F} and such that each intermediate tree is a non-crossing spanning tree. We say that TIT_{I} can be reconfigured to TFT_{F} using 𝒌k flips (or “in kk steps”) if there is a reconfiguration sequence of length at most kk. The flip distance from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} is the minimum length of a flip sequence.

The edges of TI∩TFT_{I}\cap T_{F} are called happy edges. Thus, TI∪TFT_{I}\cup T_{F} consists of the happy edges together with the symmetric difference (TI∖TF)∪(TF∖TI)(T_{I}\setminus T_{F})\cup(T_{F}\setminus T_{I}). We have |TI∖TF|=|TF∖TI||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}|=|T_{F}\setminus T_{I}|. A flip sequence of length |TI∖TF||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}| is called a perfect flip sequence. In a perfect flip sequence, every flip removes an edge of TIT_{I} and adds an edge of TFT_{F}—these are called perfect flips.

2 A two-phase reconfiguration approach

In this section we give a new algorithm to reconfigure between two non-crossing spanning trees on nn points using at most 2​n−32n-3 flips. This is basically the same as the upper bound of 2​n−42n-4 originally achieved by Avis and Fukuda [10], but the advantage of our new algorithm is that it gives a bound of 1.5​n−21.5n-2 flips when one tree is a path and either: (1) the path is monotone; or (2) the points are in convex position. Furthermore, for these two cases, we show a lower bound of 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips, so the bounds are tight up to the additive constant.

Before proceeding, we mention one way in which our upper bound result differs from some other reconfiguration bounds. Many of those bounds (i.e., upper bounds on the diameter dd of the reconfiguration graph) are actually bounds on the radius rr of the reconfiguration graph. The idea is to identify a “canonical” configuration and prove that its distance to any other configuration is at most rr, thus proving that the diameter dd is at most 2​r2r. For example, Avis and Fukuda’s 2​n2n bound is achieved via a canonical star centered at a convex hull point. As another example, the bound of O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) flips between triangulations of a point set can be proved using the Delaunay triangulation as a canonical configuration, and the bound of 2​n2n flips for the special case of points in convex position uses a canonical star triangulation [35]. For some reconfiguration graphs dd is equal to 2​r2r (e.g., for the Rubik’s cube, because of the underlying permutation group). However, in general, dd can be less than 2​r2r, in which case, using a canonical configuration will not give the best diameter bound. Indeed, our result does not use a canonical configuration, and we do not bound the radius of the reconfiguration graph.

Our algorithm has two phases. In the first phase, we reconfigure the input trees in a total of at most n−2n-2 flips so that one is “upward” and one is “downward” (this is where we save if one tree is a path). In the second phase we show that an upward tree can be reconfigured to a downward tree in n−1n-1 flips. We begin by defining these terms.

Let PP be a set of nn points in general position. Order the points v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n} by increasing yy-coordinate (if necessary, we slightly perturb the point set to ensure that no two yy-coordinates are identical). Let TT be a non-crossing spanning tree of PP. Imagining the edges as directed upward, we call a vertex viv_{i} a sink if there are no edges in TT connecting viv_{i} to a higher vertex vj,j>iv_{j},j>i, and we call viv_{i} a source if there are no edges connecting viv_{i} to a lower vertex vk,k<iv_{k},k<i. We call TT a downward tree if it has only one sink (which must then be vnv_{n}) and we call TT an upward tree if it has only one source (which must then be v1v_{1}). Observe that in a downward tree every vertex except vnv_{n} has exactly one edge connected to a higher vertex, and in an upward tree every vertex except v1v_{1} has exactly one edge connected to a lower vertex.

2.1 Phase 1: Reconfiguring to upward/downward trees

We first bound the number of flips needed to reconfigure a single tree TT to be upward or downward. If a tree has tt sinks, then we need at least t−1t-1 flips to reconfigure it to a downward tree—we show that t−1t-1 flips suffice. Note that tt is at most n−1n-1 since v1v_{1} cannot be a sink (this bound is realized by a star at v1v_{1}).

Theorem 1.

Let TT be a non-crossing spanning tree with ss sources and tt sinks. TT can be reconfigured to a downward tree with t−1≤n−2t-1\leq n-2 flips. TT can be reconfigured to an upward tree with s−1≤n−2s-1\leq n-2 flips. Furthermore, these reconfiguration sequences do not flip any edge of the form vi​vi+1v_{i}v_{i+1} where 1≤i<n1\leq i<n.

Proof.

We give the proof for a downward tree, since the other case is symmetric. The proof is by induction on tt. In the base case, t=1t=1 and the tree is downward and so no flips are needed. Otherwise, let vi,1<i<nv_{i},1<i<n be a sink. The plan is to decrease tt by adding an edge going upward from viv_{i} and removing some edge vk​vl,k<lv_{k}v_{l},k<l from the resulting cycle while ensuring that vkv_{k} does not become a sink.

If there is an edge vi​vjv_{i}v_{j} that does not cross any edge of TT, we say that viv_{i} sees vjv_{j}. We argue that viv_{i} sees some vertex vjv_{j} with j>ij>i. If viv_{i} sees vnv_{n}, then choose j=nj=n. Otherwise the upward ray directed from viv_{i} to vnv_{n} hits some edge ee before it reaches vnv_{n}. Continuously rotate the ray around viv_{i} towards the higher endpoint of ee until the ray reaches the endpoint or is blocked by some other vertex. In either case this gives us a vertex vjv_{j} visible from viv_{i} and higher than viv_{i}. For example, in Figure 1, the sink v5v_{5} sees v7v_{7}.

Adding the edge vi​vjv_{i}v_{j} to TT creates a cycle. Let vkv_{k} be the lowest vertex in the cycle. Then vkv_{k} has two upward edges, and in particular, k<ik<i. Remove the edge vk​vlv_{k}v_{l} that goes higher up. Then vkv_{k} does not become a sink, and furthermore, if the edge vk​vk+1v_{k}v_{k+1} is in TT, then we do not remove it. ∎

Since no vertex is both a sink and a source, any tree has s+t≤ns+t\leq n, which yields the following result that will be useful later on when we reconfigure between a path and a tree.

Corollary 2.

Let TT be a non-crossing spanning tree. Then either TT can be reconfigured to a downward tree in 0.5​n−10.5n-1 flips or TT can be reconfigured to an upward tree in 0.5​n−10.5n-1 flips. Furthermore, these reconfiguration sequences do not flip any edge of the form vi​vi+1v_{i}v_{i+1} where 1≤i<n1\leq i<n.

We next bound the number of flips needed to reconfigure two given trees into opposite trees, meaning that one tree is upward and one is downward. By Theorem 1, we can easily do this in at most 2​n−42n-4 flips (using n−2n-2 flips to reconfigure each tree independently). We now show that n−2n-2 flips suffice to reconfigure the two trees into opposite trees.

Theorem 3.

Given two non-crossing spanning trees on the same point set, we can flip them into opposite trees in at most n−2n-2 flips.

Proof.

Let the trees be T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}, and let sis_{i} and tit_{i} be the number of sources and sinks of TiT_{i}, for i=1,2i=1,2. Since si+ti≤ns_{i}+t_{i}\leq n, we have s1+t1+s2+t2≤2​ns_{1}+t_{1}+s_{2}+t_{2}\leq 2n. This implies that s1+t2≤ns_{1}+t_{2}\leq n or t1+s2≤nt_{1}+s_{2}\leq n. In the former case use Theorem 1 to flip T1T_{1} upward and T2T_{2} downward in s1−1+t2−1≤n−2s_{1}-1+t_{2}-1\leq n-2 flips; otherwise flip T1T_{1} downward and T2T_{2} upward in t1−1+s2−1≤n−2t_{1}-1+s_{2}-1\leq n-2 flips. ∎

2.2 Phase 2: Reconfiguring an upward tree into a downward tree

In this section we show how to reconfigure from an initial downward tree TIT_{I} to a final upward tree TFT_{F} on a general point set using only perfect flips. Thus the total number of flips will be |TI∖TF||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}|. The sequence of flips is simple to describe, and it will be obvious that each flip yields a spanning tree. What needs proving is that each intermediate tree is non-crossing. To simplify the description of the algorithm, imagine TIT_{I} colored red and TFT_{F} colored blue. Refer to Figure 2. Recall that v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n} is the ordering of the points by increasing yy-coordinate. Define bib_{i} to be the (unique) blue edge in TFT_{F} going down from viv_{i}, i=2,…,ni=2,\dots,n. An unhappy edge is an edge of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F}, i.e., it is red but not blue.

Reconfiguration algorithm.

Let T1=TIT_{1}=T_{I}. For i=2,…,ni=2,\ldots,n we create a tree TiT_{i} that contains b2,…,bib_{2},\ldots,b_{i} and all the happy edges. If bib_{i} is happy, then bib_{i} is already in the current tree and we simply set Ti:=Ti−1T_{i}:=T_{i-1}. Otherwise, consider the cycle formed by adding bib_{i} to Ti−1T_{i-1} and, in this cycle, let rir_{i} be the unhappy red edge with the lowest bottom endpoint. Note that rir_{i} exists, otherwise all edges in the cycle would be blue. Set Ti:=Ti−1∪{bi}∖{ri}T_{i}:=T_{i-1}\cup\{b_{i}\}\setminus\{r_{i}\}.

This reconfiguration algorithm, applied to the trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} from Figure 2, is depicted in Figure 3.

Theorem 4.

Given a red downward tree TIT_{I} and a blue upward tree TFT_{F} on a general point set, the reconfiguration algorithm described above flips TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} using |TI∖TF||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}| perfect flips.

Proof.

It is clear that each TiT_{i} is a spanning tree, and that each flip is perfect, so the number of flips is |TI∖TF||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}|. In particular, a happy edge is never removed, so TiT_{i} contains all happy edges. We must show that each TiT_{i} is non-crossing. By induction, it suffices to show that if step i≥2i\geq 2 adds edge bib_{i} and removes edge rir_{i}, then bib_{i} does not cross any edge of Ti−1T_{i-1} except possibly rir_{i}. We examine the structure of Ti−1T_{i-1}.

Let Bi−1B_{i-1} be the subtree with edges b2,…,bi−1b_{2},\ldots,b_{i-1}. Note that Bi−1B_{i-1} is connected. By construction, Ti−1T_{i-1} contains Bi−1B_{i-1} and all the other edges of Ti−1T_{i-1} are red. Let Ri−1R_{i-1} consist of vertices vi,…,vnv_{i},\ldots,v_{n} and the edges of Ti−1T_{i-1} induced on those vertices. The edges of Ri−1R_{i-1} are red, and Ri−1R_{i-1} consists of some connected components (possibly isolated vertices). In Ti−1T_{i-1} each component of Ri−1R_{i-1} has exactly one red connector-edge joining it to Bi−1B_{i-1}. Thus Ti−1T_{i-1} consists of Bi−1B_{i-1}, Ri−1R_{i-1}, and the connector-edges for the components of Ri−1R_{i-1}.

Now consider the flip performed to create TiT_{i} by adding edge bib_{i} and removing edge rir_{i}. Since bib_{i} is a blue edge, it cannot cross any edge of Bi−1B_{i-1}. Since bib_{i}’s topmost vertex is viv_{i}, bib_{i} cannot cross any edge of Ri−1R_{i-1}. Furthermore, bib_{i} cannot cross a happy edge. Thus the only remaining possibility is for bib_{i} to cross an unhappy connector-edge.

We will prove:

Claim 5.

If Ri−1R_{i-1} is disconnected, then all connector-edges are happy.

Assuming the claim, we only need to show that bib_{i} is non-crossing when Ri−1R_{i-1} is connected. Then there is only one connector-edge rr joining Ri−1R_{i-1} to Bi−1B_{i-1}. If rr is happy, then bib_{i} cannot cross it. So assume that rr is unhappy. Refer to Figure 4(a). Now, the cycle γ\gamma in Ti−1∪{bi}T_{i-1}\cup\{b_{i}\} contains rr, since bib_{i} and rr are the only edges between Ri−1R_{i-1} and Bi−1B_{i-1}. Of the red edges in γ\gamma, rr is the one with the lowest bottom endpoint. This implies that rr is chosen as rir_{i}, and removed. Therefore bib_{i} does not cross any edges of TiT_{i}, so TiT_{i} is non-crossing.

It remains to prove the claim. Let CC be a connected component of Ri−1R_{i-1}, and let rr be its connector-edge. Refer to Figure 4(b). We must prove that rr is happy. In the initial red tree TIT_{I}, the vertices vi,…,vnv_{i},\ldots,v_{n} induce a connected subtree, so CC and Ri−1∖CR_{i-1}\setminus C were once connected. Suppose they first became disconnected by the removal of red edge rjr_{j} in step jj of the algorithm, for some j<ij<i. Consider the blue edge bjb_{j} that was added in step jj of the algorithm, and the cycle γj\gamma_{j} in Tj−1∪{bj}T_{j-1}\cup\{b_{j}\}. Now γj\gamma_{j} must contain another edge, call it ee, with one endpoint in CC and one endpoint, vkv_{k}, not in CC. Note that ee is red since it has an endpoint in CC, and note that vkv_{k} is not in Ri−1∖CR_{i-1}\setminus C otherwise CC and Ri−1∖CR_{i-1}\setminus C would not be disconnected after the removal of rjr_{j}. Therefore vkv_{k} must lie in Bi−1B_{i-1}, i.e., k≤i−1k\leq i-1. If ee is unhappy, then in step jj the algorithm would prefer to remove ee instead of rjr_{j} since ee is a red edge in γj\gamma_{j} with a lower bottom endpoint. So ee is happy, which means that the algorithm never removes it, and it is contained in Ti−1T_{i-1}. Therefore ee must be equal to rr, the unique connector-edge in Ti−1T_{i-1} between CC and Bi−1B_{i-1}. Therefore rr is happy. ∎

2.3 Two-phase reconfiguration algorithm

We can now combine the results of Sections 2.1 and 2.2 to develop a new two-phase reconfiguration algorithm between two non-crossing spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}:

  1. 1.

    In the first phase we reconfigure TIT_{I} into TI′T^{\prime}_{I} and TFT_{F} into TF′T^{\prime}_{F} such that TI′T^{\prime}_{I} and TF′T^{\prime}_{F} are opposite trees (one upward and one downward), using Theorem 3.

  2. 2.

    In the second phase we reconfigure TI′T^{\prime}_{I} into TF′T^{\prime}_{F} using only perfect flips, as given by Theorem 4. (Note, however, that the happy edges in TI′T^{\prime}_{I} and TF′T^{\prime}_{F} may differ from the ones in TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, since the first phase does not preserve happy edges).

Finally, we concatenate the reconfiguration sequences from TIT_{I} to TI′T^{\prime}_{I}, from TI′T^{\prime}_{I} to TF′T^{\prime}_{F}, and the reverse of the sequence from TFT_{F} to TF′T^{\prime}_{F}.

Theorem 6.

If TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} are non-crossing spanning trees on a general point set, then the algorithm presented above reconfigures TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} in at most 2​n−32n-3 flips.

Proof.

By Theorem 3, the first phase of the algorithm takes at most n−2n-2 flips. By Theorem 4, the second phase uses at most n−1n-1 flips. It follows that the total number of flips is at most 2​n−32n-3. ∎

Theorem 7.

For a general point set, if TIT_{I} is a non-crossing spanning tree and TFT_{F} is a non-crossing path that is monotone in some direction, then TIT_{I} can be reconfigured to TFT_{F} in at most 1.5​n−2−h1.5n-2-h flips, where h=|TI∩TF|h=|T_{I}\cap T_{F}| is the number of happy edges. Furthermore, there is a lower bound of 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips, even for points in convex position and if one tree is a monotone path.

Proof.

Rotate the plane so that TFT_{F} is yy-monotone. Note that TFT_{F} is then both an upward and a downward tree. We thus have the flexibility to turn TIT_{I} into either an upward or a downward tree in the first phase of the algorithm. By Corollary 2, TIT_{I} can be turned into an upward or downward tree TI′T^{\prime}_{I} in at most 0.5​n−10.5n-1 flips. Furthermore, since TFT_{F} is a yy-monotone path, any edge in TI∩TFT_{I}\cap T_{F} has the form vi​vi+1v_{i}v_{i+1} for some 1≤i<n1\leq i<n, and thus, by Corollary 2, these edges do not flip, which implies that they are still in TI′∩TFT^{\prime}_{I}\cap T_{F}, so |TI′∩TF|≥h|T^{\prime}_{I}\cap T_{F}|\geq h. The second phase of the algorithm uses |TI′∖TF|≤n−1−h|T_{I}^{\prime}\setminus T_{F}|\leq n-1-h perfect flips to reconfigure TI′T^{\prime}_{I} into TFT_{F}. Hence the total number of flips is at most 1.5​n−2−h1.5n-2-h.

For the lower bound, see Lemma 8 below. ∎

Lemma 8.

On any set of n≥4n\geq 4 points in convex position, for nn even, there exists a non-crossing spanning tree TIT_{I} and a non-crossing path TFT_{F} such that reconfiguring TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} requires at least 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips, and this bound is tight.

Proof.

Our construction is depicted in Figure 5. Note that the tree TIT_{I} is the same as in the lower bound of 1.5​n−51.5n-5 proved by Hernando et al. [20], but their tree TFT_{F} was not a path.

The construction is as follows (refer to Figure 5(a) and (c)). The points v1​…​vnv_{1}\ldots v_{n} (ordered by increasing yy-coordinate) are placed in convex position on alternate sides of v1​vnv_{1}v_{n}. TIT_{I} contains edges v1​v2​i+1v_{1}v_{2i+1} and vn​v2​iv_{n}v_{2i} for i=1,…,n/2−1i=1,\ldots,n/2-1, and v1​vnv_{1}v_{n}. Note that v1v_{1} and vnv_{n} have degree n/2n/2 each. TFT_{F} is a path that connects vertices in order (so it includes edges vi​vi+1v_{i}v_{i+1}, for i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1).

Note that every non-hull edge of TFT_{F} (in blue) crosses at least n/2−1n/2-1 edges of TIT_{I} (in red). Indeed, edges of the form v2​i+1​v2​iv_{2i+1}v_{2i} cross exactly n/2n/2 edges: n/2−i−1n/2-i-1 edges incident to v1v_{1}, plus i+1i+1 edges incident to vnv_{n}, minus 11 because v1​vnv_{1}v_{n} is included in both counts. Edges of the form v2​i​v2​i+1v_{2i}v_{2i+1} cross one less edge (specifically v1​v2​i+1v_{1}v_{2i+1}).

Thus, any valid reconfiguration from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} must flip n/2−1n/2-1 edges of TIT_{I} out of the way before the first of the n−3n-3 non-hull edges of TFT_{F} is added. After that, we need at least one flip for each of the remaining n−4n-4 non-hull edges of TFT_{F}. Thus the total number of flips is at least n/2−1+(n−4)=1.5​n−5n/2-1+(n-4)=1.5n-5.

We note that our two-phase reconfiguration algorithm uses 1.5​n−31.5n-3 flips for this instance, but there is a flip sequence of length 1.5​n−51.5n-5: first flip v2​vnv_{2}v_{n} to v1​v2v_{1}v_{2} to create a happy hull edge, then connect vnv_{n} to all viv_{i} for odd i≥7i\geq 7 by performing the flips v1​viv_{1}v_{i} to vn​viv_{n}v_{i} in order of decreasing ii. The number of flips thus far is n/2−2n/2-2 (note that v1​v3v_{1}v_{3} and v1​v5v_{1}v_{5} stay in place). The resulting tree (shown in Figure 5b) has two happy hull edges. We show that this tree can be reconfigured into TFT_{F} using perfect flips only (so the number of flips is n−3n-3). Flip v1​vnv_{1}v_{n} to non-hull edge v4​v5v_{4}v_{5} and view the resulting tree as the union of an upward tree rooted at v1v_{1} and a downward subtree rooted at vnv_{n} (sharing v4​v5v_{4}v_{5}). These two subtrees are separated by v4​v5v_{4}v_{5} and therefore can be independently reconfigured into their corresponding subtrees in TFT_{F} using perfect flips, as given by Theorem 4. Thus the total number of flips is (n/2−2)+(n−3)=1.5​n−5(n/2-2)+(n-3)=1.5n-5, proving this bound tight. ∎

Theorem 9.

For points in convex position, if TIT_{I} is a non-crossing spanning tree and TFT_{F} is a path, then TIT_{I} can be reconfigured to TFT_{F} in at most 1.5​n−2−h1.5n-2-h flips, where h=|TI∩TF|h=|T_{I}\cap T_{F}| is the number of happy edges. Furthermore, there is a lower bound of 1.5​n−51.5n-5 flips.

Proof.

When points are in convex position, two edges cross (a geometric property) if and only if their endpoints alternate in the cyclic ordering of points around the convex hull (a combinatorial property). This insight allows us to show that the path TFT_{F} is “equivalent to” a monotone path, which means that we can use the previous Theorem 7. In particular, let the ordering of points in TFT_{F} be v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n}. We claim that the above algorithms can be applied using this ordering in place of the ordering of points by yy-coordinate. Thus, a sink in TIT_{I} is a point viv_{i} with no edge to a later vertex in the ordering, and etc. One could justify this by examining the steps of the algorithms (we relied on geometry only to show that we can add a non-crossing edge “upward” from a sink, which becomes easy for points in convex position). As an alternative, we make the argument formal by showing how to perturb the points so that TFT_{F} becomes a monotone path while preserving the ordering of points around the convex hull—which justifies that the flips for the perturbed points are correct for the original points.

First adjust the points so that they lie on a circle with v1v_{1} lowest at yy-coordinate 1 and vnv_{n} highest at yy-coordinate nn. The convex hull separates into two chains from v1v_{1} to vnv_{n}. Observe that TFT_{F} visits the points of each chain in order from bottom to top (if aa appears before bb on one chain but TFT_{F} visits bb before aa, then the subpaths from v1v_{1} to bb and from aa to vnv_{n} would cross). Thus, we can place viv_{i} at yy-coordinate ii while preserving the ordering of points around the circle.

We can now apply Theorem 7 to TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} on the perturbed points. This gives a sequence of at most 1.5​n−h−21.5n-h-2 flips to reconfigure TIT_{I} into TFT_{F} and the flip sequence is still correct on the original points, thus proving the upper bound claimed by the theorem. For the lower bound, note that the points in Figure 5 are in convex position and TFT_{F} is a path. Thus Lemma 8 (which employs the example from Figure 5) settles the lower bound claim. ∎

3 Improving the Upper Bound for a Convex Point Set

In this section we show that for nn points in convex position, reconfiguration between two non-crossing spanning trees can always be done with fewer than 2​n2n flips.

Theorem 10.

There is an algorithm to reconfigure between an initial non-crossing spanning tree TIT_{I} and a final non-crossing spanning tree TFT_{F} on nn points in convex position using at most 2​d−Ω⁡(log⁡d)2d-\Omega(\log d) flips, where d=|TI∖TF|d=|T_{I}\setminus T_{F}|.

Before proving the theorem we note that previous reconfiguration algorithms do not respect this bound. Avis and Fukuda [10, Section 3.7] proved an upper bound of 2​n2n minus a constant by reconfiguring each spanning tree TiT_{i} to a star SS using |S∖Ti||S\setminus T_{i}| flips. When TiT_{i} is a path, |S∩Ti|≤2|S\cap T_{i}|\leq 2, so |S∖Ti|≥n−3|S\setminus T_{i}|\geq n-3 and their method takes at least 2​n−62n-6 flips. Similarly, the method of flipping both trees to a canonical path around the convex hull takes at least 2​n−62n-6 flips when T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} are paths with only two edges on the convex hull. Although paths behave badly for these canonicalization methods, they are actually easy cases as we showed in Section 2. As in that section, we do not use a canonical tree to prove Theorem 10—instead, the flips are tailored to the specific initial and final trees.

Throughout this section, we assume points in convex position. Consider the symmetric difference D=(TI∖TF)∪(TF∖TI)D=(T_{I}\setminus T_{F})\cup(T_{F}\setminus T_{I}), so |D|=2​d|D|=2d. It is easy to reconfigure TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} using 2​d2d flips—we use dd flips to move the edges of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F} to the convex hull, giving an intermediate tree TT, and, from the other end, use dd flips to move the edges of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I} to the same tree TT. The plan is to save Ω⁡(log⁡d)\Omega(\log d) of these flips by using that many perfect flips (recall that a perfect flip exchanges an edge of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F} directly with an edge of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I}). In more detail, the idea is to find an edge e∈De\in D that is crossed by at most (roughly) d/2d/2 edges of the other tree. We flip all but one of the crossing edges out of the way to the convex hull, and—if ee is chosen carefully—we show that we can perform one flip from ee to the last crossing edge, thus providing one perfect flip after at most d/2d/2 flips. Repeating this approach log⁡d\log d times gives our claimed bound.

We first show how to find an edge ee with not too many crossings. To do this, we define “minimal” edges. An edge joining points uu and vv determines two subsets of points, those clockwise from uu to vv and those clockwise from vv to uu (both sets include uu and vv). We call these the sides of the edge. An edge is contained in a side if both endpoints are in the side. We call a side minimal if it contains no edge of the symmetric difference DD, and call an edge e∈De\in D minimal if at least one of its sides is minimal. Note that if DD is non-empty then it contains at least one minimal edge (possibly a convex hull edge). We need the following property of minimal edges.

Claim 11.

Let e=u​ve=uv be a minimal edge of DD. Let QQ be a minimal side of ee, and let Q¯\bar{Q} be the other side. Suppose e∈TFe\in T_{F}. Then TI∩QT_{I}\cap Q consists of exactly two connected components, one containing uu and one containing vv.

Proof.

The set TF∩QT_{F}\cap Q is a non-crossing tree consisting of edge ee and two subtrees TuT_{u} containing uu and TvT_{v} containing vv. Since ee is minimal, there are no edges of DD in QQ except for ee itself. This means that TI∩QT_{I}\cap Q consists of TuT_{u} and TvT_{v}, and since e∉TIe\notin T_{I}, these two components of TI∩QT_{I}\cap Q are disconnected in QQ. See Figure 6(a). ∎

Our algorithm will operate on a minimal edge ee. To guarantee the savings in flips, we need a minimal edge with not too many crossings.

Lemma 12.

If DD is non-empty, then there is a minimal edge with at most ⌊(d+3)/2⌋\lfloor(d+3)/2\rfloor crossings.

Proof.

Clearly the lemma holds if some minimal edge is not crossed at all (e.g., a convex hull edge in DD), so we assume that all minimal edges have a crossing. Let aa be a minimal edge of DD. Suppose a∈TFa\in T_{F}. Let AA be a minimal side of aa, and let A¯\bar{A} be the other side. Our plan is to find a second minimal edge b∈TFb\in T_{F} such that bb is inside A¯\bar{A} and bb has a minimal side BB that is contained in A¯\bar{A}. We will then argue that aa or bb satisfies the lemma. See Figure 6(b).

If A¯\bar{A} is minimal, then set b:=ab:=a and B=A¯B=\bar{A}. Otherwise, let bb be an edge of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I} in A¯\bar{A} whose BB side (the side in A¯\bar{A}) contains no other edge of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I}. Note that bb exists, and that all the edges of TFT_{F} in BB (except bb) lie in TIT_{I}. If bb is not minimal, then BB contains a minimal edge cc (which must then be in TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F}), and cc is not crossed by any edge of TFT_{F}, because such an edge would either have to cross bb, which is impossible since b∈TFb\in T_{F}, or lie in BB, which is impossible since all the edges of TFT_{F} in B∖{b}B\setminus\{b\} are in TF∩TIT_{F}\cap T_{I}. But we assumed that all minimal edges are crossed, so cc cannot exist, and so bb must be minimal.

Let kak_{a} be the number of edges of TIT_{I} crossing aa, let kbk_{b} be the number of edges of TIT_{I} crossing bb, and let ka​bk_{ab} be the number of edges of TIT_{I} crossing both aa and bb. Observe that ka+kb≤d+ka​bk_{a}+k_{b}\leq d+k_{ab}.

We claim that ka​b≤3k_{ab}\leq 3. Then ka+kb≤d+3k_{a}+k_{b}\leq d+3 so min⁡{ka,kb}≤(d+3)/2\min\{k_{a},k_{b}\}\leq(d+3)/2, which will complete the proof since the number of crossings is an integer. By Claim 11, TI∩AT_{I}\cap A has two connected components and TI∩BT_{I}\cap B has two connected components. Now 4 connected components in a tree can have at most three edges joining them, which implies that ka​b≤3k_{ab}\leq 3. (Note that this argument is correct even for a=ba=b, though we get a sharper bound since ka=kb=ka​b≤3k_{a}=k_{b}=k_{ab}\leq 3.) ∎

Algorithm.

Choose a minimal edge ee with kk crossings, where 0≤k≤(d+3)/20\leq k\leq(d+3)/2 (as guaranteed by Lemma 12). Suppose e∈TFe\in T_{F}, so the crossing edges belong to TIT_{I}. The case where e∈TIe\in T_{I} is symmetric. In either case the plan is to perform some flips on TIT_{I} and some on TFT_{F} to reduce the difference dd by kk (or by 1, if k=0k=0) and apply the algorithm recursively to the resulting instance. Note that the algorithm constructs a flip sequence by adding flips at both ends of the sequence.

If k=0k=0 then add ee to TIT_{I}. This creates a cycle, and the cycle must have an edge ff in TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F}. Remove ff. This produces a new tree TIT_{I}. We have performed one perfect flip and reduced dd by 1. Now recurse.

Next suppose k≥1k\geq 1. Let e=u​ve=uv. Let QQ be the minimal side of ee and let Q¯\bar{Q} be the other side (both sets include uu and vv). Let f1,…,fkf_{1},\ldots,f_{k} be the edges that cross ee. We will flip all but the last crossing edge to the convex hull. For i=1,…​k−1i=1,\ldots k-1 we flip fif_{i} as follows.

  1. 1.

    Perform a flip in TIT_{I} by removing fif_{i} and adding a convex hull edge gg that lies in Q¯\bar{Q}. (The existence of gg is proved below.)

  2. 2.

    If g∈TFg\in T_{F} then this was a perfect flip and we have performed one perfect flip and reduced dd by 1.

  3. 3.

    Otherwise (if g∉TFg\notin T_{F}), perform a flip in TFT_{F} by adding gg and removing an edge h∈TF∖TIh\in T_{F}\setminus T_{I}, that lies in Q¯\bar{Q} and is not equal to ee. (The existence of hh is proved below.)

At this point, only fkf_{k} crosses ee. Perform one flip in TIT_{I} to remove fkf_{k} and add ee. (Correctness proved below.) Now, apply the algorithm recursively to the resulting TI,TFT_{I},T_{F}.

This completes the description of the algorithm.

Correctness.

We must prove that gg and hh exist and that the final flip is valid.

First note that ee remains a minimal edge after each flip performed inside the loop because we never add or remove edges inside QQ. We need one more invariant of the loop.

Claim 13.

Throughout the loop uu and vv are disconnected in TI∩Q¯T_{I}\cap{\bar{Q}}.

Proof.

Suppose there is a path π\pi from uu to vv in TI∩Q¯T_{I}\cap{\bar{Q}}. Now consider the edge fkf_{k} which crosses ee, say from x∈Qx\in Q to y∈Q¯y\in{\bar{Q}}. Since fkf_{k} cannot cross π\pi, we have y∈πy\in\pi. By Claim 11, TI∩QT_{I}\cap Q consists of two components, one containing uu and one containing vv. Suppose, without loss of generality, that xx lies in the component containing uu. Then there is a path from xx to uu in TI∩QT_{I}\cap Q and a path from uu to yy in TI∩Q¯T_{I}\cap{\bar{Q}}, and these paths together with fkf_{k} make a cycle in TIT_{I}, a contradiction. ∎

First we prove that gg exists in Step 1. Removing fif_{i} from TIT_{I} disconnects TIT_{I} into two pieces. There are two convex hull edges that connect the two pieces. By Claim 11, TI∩QT_{I}\cap Q consists of two connected components, one containing uu and one containing vv. Thus at most one of the convex hull edges lies in QQ, so at least one lies in Q¯\bar{Q}.

Next we prove that hh exists in Step 3. Adding gg to TFT_{F} creates a cycle γ\gamma in TFT_{F} and this cycle must lie in Q¯\bar{Q} (because e∈TFe\in T_{F}) and must contain at least one edge of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I} (because TIT_{I} does not contain a cycle). If ee were the only edge of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I} in γ\gamma, then uu and vv would be joined by a path in TI∩Q¯T_{I}\cap{\bar{Q}}, contradicting Claim 13. Thus hh exists.

Finally, we prove that the last flip in TIT_{I} (to remove fkf_{k} and add ee) is valid. Removing fkf_{k} leaves uu and vv disconnected in QQ by Claim 11 and disconnected in Q¯\bar{Q} by Claim 13. Adding ee reconnects them, and yields a non-crossing spanning tree.

Analysis.

We now prove that the algorithm uses at most the claimed number of flips.

Observation 14.

In each recursive call: if k=0k=0, then the algorithm performs one perfect flip and reduces dd by 1; and if k>0k>0, then the algorithm performs at most 2​k−12k-1 flips (one for fkf_{k} and at most 2 for each other fif_{i}) and reduces dd by kk (in each loop iteration, gg joins the happy set TI∩TFT_{I}\cap T_{F} and in the final step ee joins the happy set).

Lemma 15.

The number of flips performed by the algorithm is at most 2​d−⌊log⁡(d+3)⌋+12d-\lfloor\log(d{+}3)\rfloor+1.

Proof.

We prove this by induction on dd. In the base case d=0d=0 we perform 0=2​d−⌊log⁡(d+3)⌋+10=2d-\lfloor\log(d{+}3)\rfloor+1 flips.

Now assume d≥1d\geq 1, and consider what happens in the first recursive call of the algorithm, see Observation 14. If the algorithm chooses an edge with k=0k=0 crossings, then the algorithm performs one perfect flip. The resulting instance has a difference set of size d′=d−1d^{\prime}=d-1 and induction applies, so in the total number of flips we perform is at most

1+2​d′−⌊log⁡(d′+3)⌋+1=2​d−⌊log⁡(d+2)⌋≤2​d−⌊log⁡(d+3)⌋+1,\displaystyle 1+2d^{\prime}-\lfloor\log(d^{\prime}{+}3)\rfloor+1=2d-\lfloor\log(d{+}2)\rfloor\leq 2d-\lfloor\log(d{+}3)\rfloor+1,

which proves the result in this case.

Now suppose that the algorithm chooses an edge with k≥1k\geq 1 crossings, where k≤⌊(d+3)/2⌋k\leq\lfloor(d{+}3)/2\rfloor. The algorithm performs at most 2​k−12k-1 flips and the resulting instance has a difference set of size d′=d−kd^{\prime}=d-k and therefore d′+3≥d+3−⌊(d+3)/2⌋=⌈(d+3)/2⌉≥(d+3)/2d^{\prime}{+}3\geq d{+}3-\lfloor(d{+}3)/2\rfloor=\lceil(d{+}3)/2\rceil\geq(d{+}3)/2. By induction, the total number of flips that we perform is hence at most

(2​k−1)+(2​d′−⌊log⁡(d′+3)⌋+1)\displaystyle(2k-1)+(2d^{\prime}-\lfloor\log(d^{\prime}{+}3)\rfloor+1) ≤(2​k−1)+(2​(d−k)−⌊log⁡((d+3)/2)⌋+1)\displaystyle\leq(2k-1)+(2(d-k)-\lfloor\log((d{+}3)/2)\rfloor+1)
≤2​d−⌊log⁡((d+3)/2)⌋\displaystyle\leq~2d-\lfloor\log((d{+}3)/2)\rfloor
≤2​d−⌊log⁡(d+3)⌋+1\displaystyle\leq 2d-\lfloor\log(d{+}3)\rfloor+1

as desired. ∎

This completes the proof of Theorem 10.

4 The Happy Edge Conjecture

In this section we make some conjectures and prove some preliminary results in attempts to characterize which edges need to be flipped in minimum flip sequences for non-crossing spanning trees.

Recall that an edge ee is happy if ee lies in TI∩TFT_{I}\cap T_{F}. We make the following conjecture for points in convex position. In fact, we do not have a counterexample even for general point sets, though our guess is that the conjecture fails in the general case.

Conjecture 16.

[Happy Edge Conjecture for Convex Point Sets] For any point set PP in convex position and any two non-crossing spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} of PP, there is a minimum flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} such that no happy edge is flipped during the sequence.

In this section we first prove this conjecture for the case of happy edges on the convex hull. Then in Section 4.1 we make some stronger conjectures about which extra edges (outside TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}) might be needed in minimum flip sequences. In Section 4.2 we show that even if no extra edges are needed, it may be tricky to find a minimum flip sequence—or, at least, a greedy approach fails. Finally, in Section 4.3 we prove that the Happy Edge Conjecture fails if we restrict the flips to “slides” where one endpoint of the flipped edge is fixed and the other endpoint moves along an adjacent tree edge.

If the Happy Edge Conjecture is false then a minimum flip sequence might need to remove an edge and later add it back. We are able to prove something about such “remove-add” subsequences, even for general point sets:

Proposition 17.

Consider any point set PP and any two non-crossing spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} on PP and any minimum flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F}. If some edge ee is removed and later added back, then some flip during that subsequence must add an edge ff that crosses ee.

Before proving this Proposition, we note the implication that the Happy Edge Conjecture is true for convex hull edges:

Corollary 18.

Conjecture 16 is true for happy edges on the convex hull. Furthermore, every minimum flip sequence keeps the happy convex hull edges throughout the sequence.

Proof.

Let ee be a happy convex hull edge. Suppose for a contradiction that there is a minimum flip sequence in which ee is removed. Note that ee must be added back, since it is in TFT_{F}. By Proposition 17, the flip sequence must use an edge ff that crosses ee. But that is impossible because ee is a convex hull edge so nothing crosses it. ∎

Proof of Proposition 17.

Consider a flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} and suppose that an edge ee is removed and later added back, and that no edge crossing ee is added during that subsequence. We will make a shorter flip sequence. The argument is similar to the “normalization” technique used by Sleator et al. [35] to prove the happy edge result for flips in triangulations of a convex point set.

Let T0,…,TkT_{0},\ldots,T_{k} be the trees in the subsequence, where T0T_{0} and TkT_{k} contain ee, but none of the intervening trees do. Suppose that none of the trees TiT_{i} contains an edge that crosses ee. We will construct a shorter flip sequence from T0T_{0} to TkT_{k}. For each ii, 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k consider adding ee to TiT_{i}. For i≠0,ki\neq 0,k, this creates a cycle γi\gamma_{i}. Let fif_{i} be the first edge of γi\gamma_{i} that is removed during the flip sequence from TiT_{i} to TkT_{k}. Note that fif_{i} exists since TkT_{k} contains ee, so it cannot contain all of γi\gamma_{i}. Define Ni=Ti∪{e}∖{fi}N_{i}=T_{i}\cup\{e\}\setminus\{f_{i}\} for 1≤i≤k−11\leq i\leq k-1, and define N0:=T0N_{0}:=T_{0}. Observe that NiN_{i} is a spanning tree, and is non-crossing because no edge of TiT_{i} crosses ee by hypothesis. Furthermore, Nk−1=TkN_{k-1}=T_{k} because the flip from Tk−1T_{k-1} to TkT_{k} is exactly the same as the flip from Tk−1T_{k-1} to Nk−1N_{k-1}.

We claim that N0,…,Nk−1N_{0},\ldots,N_{k-1} is a flip sequence. This will complete the proof, since it is a shorter flip sequence from T0T_{0} to TkT_{k}.

Consider NiN_{i} and Ni+1N_{i+1}. Suppose that the flip from TiT_{i} to Ti+1T_{i+1} adds gg and removes hh.

Recall that γi\gamma_{i} is the cycle containing ee in Ti∪eT_{i}\cup e. If hh belongs to γi\gamma_{i} then fi=hf_{i}=h, and then to get from NiN_{i} to Ni+1N_{i+1} we add gg and remove fi+1f_{i+1}. Next, suppose that hh does not belong to γi\gamma_{i}. Then the cycle γi\gamma_{i} still exists in Ti+1T_{i+1}. Now, γi+1\gamma_{i+1} is the unique cycle in Ti+1∪eT_{i+1}\cup e. Thus γi+1=γi\gamma_{i+1}=\gamma_{i}. Furthermore, fi+1f_{i+1} is by definition the first edge removed from γi+1\gamma_{i+1} in the flip sequence from Ti+1T_{i+1} to TkT_{k}. Thus fi+1=fif_{i+1}=f_{i}. Therefore, to get from NiN_{i} to Ni+1N_{i+1} we add gg and remove hh.

This shows that a single flip changes NiN_{i} to Ni+1N_{i+1}, which completes the proof. ∎

Note that the proof of Proposition 17 produces a strictly shorter flip sequence. But to prove the Happy Edge Conjecture (Conjecture 16) it would suffice to produce a flip sequence of the same length. One possible approach is to consider how remove-add pairs and add-remove pairs interleave in a flip sequence. Proposition 17 shows that a remove-add pair for edge ee must contain an add-remove pair for ff inside it. We may need to understand how the order of flips can be rearranged in a flip sequence. Such flip order rearrangements are at the heart of results on triangulation flips, both for convex point sets [35, 32] and for general point sets [24].

4.1 Extra edges used in flip sequences

Any flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} must involve flips that remove edges of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F} and flips that add edges of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I}. Recall that in a perfect flip sequence, these are the only moves and they pair up perfectly, so the number of flips is |TI∖TF||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}|. Theorem 4 gives one situation where a perfect flip sequence is possible, but typically (e.g., in the example of Figure 5) we must add edges not in TFT_{F}, and later remove them. More formally, an edge outside TI∪TFT_{I}\cup T_{F} that is used in a flip sequence is called a parking edge, with the idea that we “park” edges there temporarily.

We make two further successively stronger conjectures. They may not hold, but disproving them would give more insight.

Conjecture 19.

For any point set PP in convex position and any two non-crossing spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} of PP there is a minimum flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} that never uses a parking edge that crosses an edge of TFT_{F}.

Conjecture 20.

For a point set PP in convex position and any two non-crossing spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} on PP there is a minimum flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} that only uses parking edges from the convex hull.

Our experiments verify Conjecture 20 for n≤10n\leq 10 points, (see Observation 22). We note that Conjecture 20 cannot hold for general point sets (there just aren’t enough convex hull edges). However, we do not know if Conjecture 19 fails for general point sets.

Claim 21.

Conjecture 20 ⟹\Longrightarrow Conjecture 19 ⟹\Longrightarrow Conjecture 16.

Proof.

The first implication is clear. For the second implication we use Proposition 17. Consider the minimum flip sequence promised by Conjecture 19. If there is a happy edge e∈TI∩TFe\in T_{I}\cap T_{F} that is removed during this flip sequence, then by Proposition 17, the flip sequence must add an edge ff that crosses ee. But then ff is a parking edge that crosses an edge of TFT_{F}, a contradiction. ∎

4.2 Finding a perfect flip sequence—greedy fails

It is an open question whether there is a polynomial time algorithm to find [the length of] a minimum flip sequence between two given non-crossing spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}. A more limited goal is testing whether there is a flip sequence of length |TI∖TF||T_{I}\setminus T_{F}|—i.e., whether there is a perfect flip sequence. This is also open.

In Figure 7 we give an example to show that a greedy approach to finding a perfect flip sequence may fail. In this example there is a perfect flip sequence but a poor choice of perfect flips leads to a dead-end configuration where no further perfect flips are possible. Note that choosing perfect flips involves pairing edges of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F} with edges of TF∖TIT_{F}\setminus T_{I} as well as ordering the pairs.

4.3 The Happy Edge Conjecture fails for edge slides

Researchers have examined various restricted types of flips for non-crossing spanning trees, see [28]. An edge slide is the most restricted flip operation possible: it keeps one endpoint of the flipped edge fixed and moves the other one along an adjacent tree edge without intersecting any of the other edges or vertices of the tree. In other words, the edge that is removed, the edge that is inserted, and the edge along which the slide takes place form an empty triangle. Aichholzer et al. [7] proved that for any set PP of nn points in the plane it is possible to transform between any two non-crossing spanning trees of PP using O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) edge slides. The authors also give an example to show that Ω⁡(n2)\Omega(n^{2}) slides might be required even if the two spanning trees differ in only two edges. This example already implies that for point sets in general position the Happy Edge Conjecture fails for edge slides. We will show that this is also the case for points in convex position.

Figure 8 shows an example of two plane spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} on 88 points in convex position which can be transformed into each other with 8 slides, shown at the bottom of the figure. To obtain this short sequence we temporarily use an edge which is common to both trees to connect the two vertices aa and bb. Thus this sequence contains a non-happy slide operation, that is, an edge that is common to both, TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} is moved. When flipping from tree TIT_{I} to tree TFT_{F} by using only happy slide operations there are some useful observations. First, there can not be an edge directly connecting aa and bb, as this would cause a cycle. This implies that any edge which connects a vertex viv_{i}, 1≤i≤41\leq i\leq 4, with bb needs at least two slides to connect aa to some (possible different) vertex vjv_{j}. Moreover, the first of these edges that gets connected to aa needs at least three slides, as at the beginning this is the shortest path connecting bb to aa. Thus in total we need at least 3+2+2+2=93+2+2+2=9 happy slide operations. Figure 8(top) shows such a sequence. It is not hard to see that this example can be generalized to larger nn and implies that the Happy Edge Conjecture fails for points in convex position.

5 Exhaustive search over small point sets in convex position

For small point sets in convex position we investigated the minimum flip distance between non-crossing spanning trees by exhaustive computer search. Table 1 summarizes the obtained results. For n=3,…,12n=3,\ldots,12 we give the number of non-crossing spanning trees (which is sequence A001764 in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, https://oeis.org) and the number of reconfiguration steps between them. Moreover, we computed the maximum reconfiguration distance between two trees (the diameter of the reconfiguration graph) as well as the radius of the reconfiguration graph. We provide the same information for the special case when the trees are non-crossing spanning paths. Note that in this case the intermediate graphs can still be non-crossing spanning trees. For the case where all intermediate graphs are also non-crossing spanning paths the diameter of the reconfiguration graph for points in convex position is known to be 2​n−62n-6 for n≥5n\geq 5 [8, 17].

Results.

Our computations show that for small sets in convex position the radius of each reconfiguration graph is strictly larger than half the diameter. More precisely, for 6≤n≤126\leq n\leq 12 the diameter is ⌊1.5​n−4⌋\lfloor 1.5n-4\rfloor and the radius is n−2n-2 which would give an upper bound for the diameter of only 2​n−42n-4. But this might be an artefact of small numbers: compare for example the result of Sleator, Tarjan, and Thurston which give the upper bound of 2​n−102n-10 for the rotation distance of binary trees which is tight only for n≥13n\geq 13 [32, 35]. That the radius seems not to be suitable for obtaining a tight bound for the diameter also supports our way of bounding the diameter of the reconfiguration graph by not using a central canonical tree.

In addition to the results shown in the table, we checked, for n≤10n\leq 10, which edges are exchanged, in order to test the Happy Edge Conjecture (Conjecture 16) and whether only parking edges on the convex hull are used (Conjecture 20).

Observation 22.

For n≤10n\leq 10 points in convex position (1) the Happy Edge Conjecture is true, and (2) there are always minimum flip sequences that only use parking edges on the convex hull.

Methods.

These computations are rather time consuming, as in principle for any pair of non-crossing spanning trees (paths) the flip distance has to be computed. For an unweighted and undirected graph GG with n′n^{\prime} nodes (non-crossing spanning trees in our case) and m′m^{\prime} edges (edge exchanges in our case) the standard algorithm to compute the diameter of GG is to apply breath first search (BFS) for each node of GG. The time requirement for this simple solution is O⁡(n′​m′)O(n^{\prime}m^{\prime}). There exist several algorithms which achieve a better running time for graphs of real world applications, see e.g., [18], but in the worst case they still need O⁡(n′​m′)O(n^{\prime}m^{\prime}) time. The basic idea behind these approaches is to compute the eccentricity e⁡(v)e(v) of a node v∈Gv\in G (which is the radius as seen from this node vv), and compare this with the largest distance dd between two nodes found so far. If e⁡(v)=d/2e(v)=d/2 we know that the diameter of the graph is dd and the algorithm terminates. The difference between the various algorithms is how the nodes for computing the eccentricity and the lower bound for the diameter are chosen and the performance of the approaches are usually tested by applying them to a set of examples.

However, it turned out that by the structure of our reconfiguration graphs these approaches do not perform better than the simple textbook solution. Because the radius of the reconfiguration graph is strictly larger than half the diameter in our test cases, no algorithmic shortcut is possible.

To still be able to compute the diameter of the rather large graphs (for n=12n=12 the reconfiguration graph has 8​414​6508~414~650 nodes and 193​666​176193~666~176 edges) we make use of the inherent symmetries of our graphs. For every tree TT we can cyclically shift the labels of the vertices (by 11 to n−1n-1 steps) and/or mirror the tree to obtain another non-crossing spanning tree T′T^{\prime} of the convex point set. All trees that can be obtained this way can be grouped together. While every tree is needed in the reconfiguration graph to correctly compute shortest reconfiguration distances, by symmetry a call of BFS for any tree from the same group will result in the same eccentricity. It is thus sufficient to call BFS only for one tree of each group. For nn points this reduces the number of calls by almost a factor of 2​n2n, as the size of the group can be up to 2​n2n (some trees are self-symmetric in different ways, thus some groups have a cardinality less than 2​n2n).

For our experiments on which edges are exchanged (for Observation 22), the computations get even more involved. The reason is that these properties of edges are defined by the initial and final tree. So it can happen that a short sub-path is valid only for some, but not all, pairs of trees where we would like to use it. Moreover, for similar reasons we can not make full use of the above described symmetry. This is the reason why we have been able to test our conjectures only for sets with up to n=10n=10 points.

6 Conclusions and Open Questions

We conclude with some open questions:

  1. 1.

    We gave two algorithms to find flip sequences for non-crossing spanning trees and we bounded the length of the flip sequence. The algorithms run in polynomial time, but it would be good to optimize the run-times.

  2. 2.

    A main open question is to close the gap between 1.5​n1.5n and 2​n2n for the leading term of the diameter of the reconfiguration graph of non-crossing spanning trees.

  3. 3.

    A less-explored problem is to find the radius of the reconfiguration graph (in the worst case, as a function of nn, the number of points). Is there a lower bound of n−cn-c on the radius of the reconfiguration graph for some small constant cc?

  4. 4.

    Prove or disprove the Happy Edge Conjecture.

  5. 5.

    Is the distance problem (to find the minimum flip distance between two non-crossing spanning trees) NP-complete for general point sets? For convex point sets? A first step towards an NP-hardness reduction would be to find instances where the Happy Edge Conjecture fails.

  6. 6.

    An easier question is to test whether there is a perfect flip sequence between two non-crossing spanning trees. Can that be done in polynomial time, at least for points in convex position?

  7. 7.

    Suppose the Happy Edge Conjecture turns out to be false. Is the following problem NP-hard? Given two trees, is there a minimum flip sequence between them that does not flip happy edges?

  8. 8.

    Suppose we have a minimum flip sequence that does not flip happy edges and does not use parking edges (i.e., the flips only involve edges of the difference set D=(TI∖TF)∪(TF∖TI)D=(T_{I}\setminus T_{F})\cup(T_{F}\setminus T_{I})). Is it a perfect flip sequence?

  9. 9.

    All the questions above can be asked for the other versions of flips between non-crossing spanning trees (as discussed in Section 1.1 and surveyed in [28]).

  10. 10.

    For the convex case, what if we only care about the cyclic order of points around the convex hull, i.e., we may freely relabel the points so long as we preserve the cyclic order of the labels. This “cyclic flip distance” may be less than the standard flip distance. For example, two stars rooted at different vertices have cyclic flip distance 00 but standard flip distance n−2n-2.
